messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 28
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Social Media Manager
  trauma_type: Military
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others, Driving with Others: Driving with people, Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons, Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Avoid Physical Stress: Situations that put my body under stress
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
  Memory: Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
  Negative Appraisals: Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now, Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kevin is a 28-year-old social media manager who lives with his girlfriend in a mid-sized city, and he came to therapy at her urging after months of escalating tension between them. He had served a single deployment as a combat medic in a forward operating base in Afghanistan three years ago, and the event that now governed his inner life had unfolded over roughly forty-five minutes during a routine resupply convoy. An IED had struck the lead vehicle, and Kevin had been the first responder. He had pulled two men from the wreckage, one of whom had lost most of his right leg below the knee. Kevin had applied tourniquets, packed wounds, and held pressure on the femoral artery of a soldier whose face he could still see clearly when he closed his eyes—except that when he tried to hold that face in his mind, it broke apart into disconnected fragments: the glint of a watch, the wet sound of breathing, the color of the blood against desert sand, none of it arranging itself into a coherent story. Sometimes the emotion came without any image at all. He would be standing in his kitchen making coffee and suddenly his heart would pound, his hands would shake, and he would feel the full, raw horror of that morning without any picture in his head. The memory felt so extreme that part of him still could not believe it had actually happened to him. He would think, *This cannot be real. This did not happen to me.*

Kevin had come to believe that the experience had permanently damaged him, that he had changed for the worse and could never change back. He was certain that someone else—someone braver, someone better trained—would not have gotten into that situation in the first place, as though he had somehow failed by being present. At work, he managed three brand accounts and spent most of his day writing copy and scheduling posts, but he had developed a rigid habit of rehearsing every conversation before it happened. Before a quick call with a client or a check-in with his supervisor, he would run through possible questions and answers in his head, sometimes writing them out, because he was terrified of being caught off guard. He avoided any situation that put his body under stress: he had stopped going to the gym, stopped running, stopped even walking quickly if he felt his heart rate rise, because the feeling of physical strain reminded him of the adrenaline of that day and he could not tolerate it.

Driving had become nearly impossible unless he was alone. His girlfriend had asked him repeatedly to drive them to dinner or to visit her family, and each time he made an excuse. When he did drive alone, he flinched at every shadow on the road. Helicopters flew over the city occasionally—medical transport, news choppers—and the sound would freeze him mid-sentence, his palms slick, his throat tight. In public, he found himself scanning for visible injuries on others. A man with a cane, a woman with a bandage on her arm, a child with a scrape: each one pulled his attention and held it, and he could not look away. He avoided military uniforms and police officers, crossing streets to avoid walking near a recruiting center or a patrol car. At night, he struggled to fall asleep because he felt he needed to stay alert. He lay in bed listening, his body tense, and if his girlfriend touched him unexpectedly in the dark he would jerk away with a sharp intake of breath, which had begun to hurt her feelings.

The consequence that finally brought him to therapy was relational. His girlfriend had told him, gently but directly, that she felt like she was living with a stranger who was always on guard. She said she missed the person who used to laugh and plan weekends and reach for her hand. Kevin had no counterargument. He was afraid of what therapy might unearth—afraid that talking about the memory would make it more real, more permanent—but he was also afraid of losing her. He sat in the intake chair with his hands on his knees, his jaw tight, and said he wanted to feel like himself again, though he was not sure that version of himself still existed.
